metadata.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (He, Zhang, Ren, Sun, 2015)
metadata.framework: Residual learning via identity shortcut connections enabling training of very deep networks
metadata.source_note: Extraction based on well-known content of arXiv:1512.03385.

nodes.name: Degradation problem
nodes.statement: The degradation problem is the phenomenon where adding more layers to a deep neural network leads to higher training error (not just test error). This is not caused by overfitting, since training accuracy degrades. It indicates that deeper models are harder to optimize, not that they lack representational capacity.

nodes.name: Residual learning formulation
nodes.statement: Instead of hoping each stack of layers directly fits a desired underlying mapping $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x})$, the residual learning formulation lets the layers fit a residual mapping $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) := \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{x}$. The original mapping is then $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}$. The hypothesis is that it is easier to optimize the residual mapping than the original unreferenced mapping.

nodes.name: Identity shortcut connection
nodes.statement: A shortcut connection performs an identity mapping: the input $\mathbf{x}$ is added directly to the output of a stack of nonlinear layers. The building block is $\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \{W_i\}) + \mathbf{x}$, where $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \{W_i\})$ represents the residual mapping to be learned. The shortcut adds neither extra parameters nor computational complexity.

nodes.name: Projection shortcut for dimension matching
nodes.statement: When the dimensions of $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ differ (e.g., when changing feature map sizes), a linear projection $W_s$ is used: $\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \{W_i\}) + W_s \mathbf{x}$. In practice, $W_s$ is implemented as a $1 \times 1$ convolution with stride 2 for spatial downsampling.

nodes.name: Basic residual block
nodes.statement: The basic residual block consists of two $3 \times 3$ convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU: $\mathbf{x} \to \mathrm{Conv}(3{\times}3) \to \mathrm{BN} \to \mathrm{ReLU} \to \mathrm{Conv}(3{\times}3) \to \mathrm{BN} \to (+\mathbf{x}) \to \mathrm{ReLU}$. Used in ResNet-18 and ResNet-34.

nodes.name: Bottleneck residual block
nodes.statement: The bottleneck block uses three layers: $1 \times 1$ (reduce dimension), $3 \times 3$, and $1 \times 1$ (restore dimension). For example, a 256-d input is reduced to 64-d by the first $1 \times 1$ conv, processed by a $3 \times 3$ conv, and restored to 256-d by the final $1 \times 1$ conv. This is computationally similar to the two-layer basic block but enables deeper networks. Used in ResNet-50, ResNet-101, ResNet-152.

nodes.name: Identity mappings ease optimization (construction argument)
nodes.statement: If an identity mapping were optimal, it would be easier for the network to push the residual $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})$ to zero than to learn an identity mapping via a stack of nonlinear layers. In the extreme case where the identity mapping is sufficient, the residual formulation allows the solver to simply drive the weights of $\mathcal{F}$ toward zero.
conclusions: Residual networks should not suffer degradation with depth

nodes.name: ImageNet classification with deep residual nets
nodes.statement: On ImageNet, a plain 34-layer network has higher training error than an 18-layer plain network (degradation). ResNet-34 achieves 3.5% lower top-1 validation error than the 18-layer counterpart. ResNet-152 achieves 4.49% top-5 single-model error. An ensemble of six ResNets achieves 3.57% top-5 error, winning ILSVRC 2015.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10 with 100 and 1000+ layer networks
nodes.statement: On CIFAR-10, ResNets with over 100 layers are successfully trained. A 110-layer ResNet achieves 6.43% error. A 1202-layer ResNet trains without optimization difficulty but suffers mild overfitting (7.93% error), showing that the residual learning framework scales to extreme depths without degradation in training.

nodes.name: COCO object detection improvement
nodes.statement: Replacing the VGG-16 backbone with ResNet-101 in Faster R-CNN yields a 28% relative improvement on COCO object detection, demonstrating that the deep representations learned by ResNets transfer effectively to detection tasks.

nodes.name: ResNet training procedure
nodes.statement: ResNets are trained with SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay $10^{-4}$, mini-batch size 256. Learning rate starts at 0.1 and is divided by 10 when the error plateaus. Batch normalization is used after each convolution. No dropout is used. Data augmentation: random $224 \times 224$ crops from resized images, horizontal flips, per-pixel mean subtraction, and color augmentation.

edges.note: The residual formulation is implemented via identity shortcuts.
The degradation problem motivates the residual learning formulation.
The basic block is a concrete realization of the identity shortcut.
The bottleneck block generalizes the basic block for efficiency at greater depth.
Projection shortcuts generalize identity shortcuts to handle dimension changes.
The residual formulation justifies the optimization argument.
ImageNet experiments test the claim that residual learning eases optimization.
CIFAR-10 experiments test extreme depth scalability.
Bottleneck blocks are used in the deep ImageNet models.
The trained ResNet backbone is transferred to COCO detection.
